analysis.one_liner: Provides federal matching funds so every state can guarantee affordable, comprehensive health insurance to all its residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it died in committee when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given states federal money to cover everyone in two steps: first voluntary state plans to close the uninsured gap within four years, then a requirement that every state guarantee universal coverage by 2006. Coverage would match what federal employees get under their standard Blue Cross-Blue Shield plan, with premiums and out-of-pocket costs capped on a sliding scale by income, no denials for preexisting conditions, and employers required to pay at least 80% of workers' premiums. It also added mental health parity to Medicare, patient-protection rules, and a new institute on patient safety.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 45 million uninsured Americans the bill cited, including over 11 million children, plus low- and moderate-income families who would face hard caps on premiums and cost-sharing, people with preexisting conditions who could no longer be excluded, Medicare beneficiaries who would gain full mental health coverage, and health care workers who would get disclosure, staffing, and advance-notice protections.

how_it_helps.text: States would get federal matching grants to reach 100% coverage of eligible residents within four years of plan approval, with bonus federal percentages for states that hit the targets.
Coverage would be at least as rich as the Federal Employees Health Benefits standard Blue Cross-Blue Shield preferred provider option, including mental health and substance abuse parity.
Families below 150% of poverty would pay no premium and at most 0.5% of income in cost-sharing; even families above 300% of poverty would be capped at 7% of income combined.
Plans could not impose preexisting condition exclusions, and at least 90% of premium income (85% in the first two years) had to go to actual medical care rather than administration or profit.

Employers would have to enroll workers in state purchasing pools and contribute at least 80% of premiums (capped at 10% of wages), with employees able to sue and recover damages and attorney's fees if an employer retaliated.

Medicare enrollees would get full mental health and substance abuse parity, and the bill would federalize patient protections passed by the House in H.R. 2723, plus new disclosure, home care, and workforce notice standards.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations drawing on budget surpluses; employers, which would owe at least 80% of employee premiums (large employers choosing their own plans would owe an extra 1% of payroll); and high-income individuals and large corporations, since the bill's stated offsets include cutting federal tax benefits available only to those in the top brackets.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' as permanent budget authority for covering tens of millions of people, with no fixed price tag, so the federal cost would have been very large and hard to estimate in advance.

Every state would be forced to design and implement a universal system by 2006, and residents could sue their state in federal court if it failed, a significant federal mandate on states regardless of local preferences.
Federal payments to states would be held to premium inflation minus half a percentage point, a cost-containment squeeze that states and plans could argue underfunds the guaranteed benefit over time.
The employer mandate (80% of premiums, up to 10% of wages) would raise labor costs, which small employers in particular might absorb through slower hiring or lower wages.
Stripping ERISA protections from state-regulated plans would upend the uniform federal framework large employers have relied on since 1974, inviting litigation and administrative upheaval.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the largest kind available in health policy: guaranteed coverage and hard affordability caps for the roughly 45 million uninsured people the bill's own findings described, plus administrative savings from pooling. The costs are real and open-ended — an uncapped federal appropriation, a hard employer mandate, and a forced timeline on every state — and the bill chose to pay for it partly by cutting tax benefits for top-bracket households and large corporations. It was an ambitious, expensive design whose fiscal details had never been scored or negotiated, which is part of why it drew almost no cosponsors in the five weeks it existed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees in July 2000, passed to a health subcommittee a month later, and no one ever scheduled it for a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), joined by Rep. David Obey (D-WI), introduced the bill on July 27, 2000, in the final months of the 106th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, a dual referral that requires both committees to act before the bill can move.
On August 31, 2000, the Commerce Committee sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment; that was the bill's last action of any kind.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death left the status quo intact: the roughly 45 million uninsured remained without coverage, while employers avoided the 80% premium mandate, insurers avoided the 90% medical-loss requirement and cost caps, and top-bracket taxpayers and large corporations kept the tax benefits the bill would have trimmed. The committee chairs preserved their control over which health bills reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat, and the bill died without any action in committees chaired by Republicans, so the record shows support only from one party and no recorded opposition votes.

industries.note: The bill would have routed universal coverage through state-approved private plans and purchasing pools, making insurers permanent channels for a new public benefit — but it also forced them to spend at least 90% of premiums on care, ban preexisting-condition exclusions, cap charges by income, and bid competitively annually. Insurers would gain a huge subsidized customer base while losing pricing and coverage-denial flexibility.

Employers would have to enroll workers in state purchasing pools and pay at least 80% of premiums (capped at 10% of wages), with large employers choosing their own coverage owing an extra 1% of payroll, and with employees able to sue for damages if they retaliated. Their added cost is the coverage ordinary workers would gain.

The bill's stated payment sources include reducing federal tax benefits available only to individuals and large corporations in the top brackets, so the richest taxpayers would help fund universal coverage.

Universally covered patients would mean far less unpaid care and fewer bad debts for providers, though the bill also requires public disclosure of their financial arrangements and staffing information.
